title: Secret Tongues and How to Sort Them
description: A 12th-century abbess, an Ottoman Sufi, and the terms used to classify invented languages

concepts.title: Hildegard's Unknown Language
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 12th century Hildegard of Bingen (c. 1098 to 1179), the visionary abbess who founded a convent at Rupertsberg on the Rhine in 1150, set down a glossary of 1,011 words that no one had ever spoken. Its title presents her as a mere channel: Ignota lingua per simplicem hominem Hildegardem prolata, "an unknown language brought forth by a simple person, Hildegard." The Lingua Ignota survives in two manuscripts copied around 1200, the Wiesbaden collection of her works called the Riesenkodex and a manuscript now in Berlin, glossed in Latin and sometimes in German.

The words run down a ladder of being, starting with God and the angels, then people and family, parts of the body, diseases, church ranks, crafts, days and months, clothing, tools, and last plants, a few birds and insects. God is Aigonz, man Iur, woman Uanix, father Peueriz, mother Maiz. Almost all are nouns. There are no verbs and no grammar of its own, so in use the words would have slotted into Latin sentences. The one surviving text, her antiphon "O orzchis Ecclesia," mixes five unknown words into Latin. She also devised a 23-letter alphabet, the litterae ignotae.

Why she made it is unknown, and scholars disagree. Barbara Newman suggested it bound her nuns together as a private community language. Sarah Higley, who edited the full glossary in 2007, found no evidence that the nuns were ever taught it and reads it instead as a distillation of the cosmic order in Hildegard's visionary books. Nineteenth-century writers who called it an early universal language were projecting their own era's hopes backward.

concepts.title: Balaibalan, a Sufi Language
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the few early invented languages from outside Europe survives in dictionaries written in Arabic script in the 16th-century Ottoman world. Called Balaibalan, or Bâleybelen in modern Turkish spelling, it is mostly a priori: its roots were largely made up, though some came from Arabic and others from the imagery of Sufi poetry. The word mim, "mouth," apparently echoes the Arabic letter mim, which poets compared to a small mouth. Its grammar stacks suffixes onto roots in the Turkish manner, with habits borrowed from Persian and Arabic.

Its author was long a puzzle. Some scholars credited the Hurufis, a mystical movement founded in the 14th century by Fazlallah Astarabadi that found divine meaning in letters. In 1966 the Turkish historian Midhat Sertoğlu pointed to manuscripts in which Muhyî-i Gülşenî presents the language as his own work. Born in Edirne around 1528 and dying in the early 17th century, Muhyî was a Sufi of the Gülşenî order who spent most of his life in Cairo, serving as custodian of the order's main lodge there. He wrote some ten treatises on Balaibalan grammar and several dictionaries, one listing 392 Persian verbal nouns with Turkish, Arabic and Balaibalan equivalents. Copies are held in Paris and at Princeton, and Mustafa Koç published a critical edition in Istanbul in 2005.

Its purpose, like Hildegard's, is debated. The Turkish encyclopedia of Islam describes it as meant for Turks, Arabs and Persians alike; other scholars see a sacred or poetic language for an inner circle of mystics.

concepts.title: Sorting the Inventions
concepts.contentHtml:
A language devised by a person or group, rather than grown out of ordinary human use, is a constructed language, or conlang. In Histoire de la langue universelle (1903), which reviewed 38 projects for a world language, the French logician Louis Couturat and the mathematician Léopold Leau drew a line still in use. An a priori language builds its words and categories from first principles, as Hildegard did and as 17th-century philosophers would. An a posteriori language borrows its material from existing languages, as Esperanto does.

Conlangers today usually sort by purpose. Auxiliary languages (auxlangs), such as Volapük and Esperanto, aim to let strangers talk across borders. Engineered languages (engelangs), such as Loglan and Lojban, test an idea about logic or the mind. Artistic languages (artlangs), such as Tolkien's Elvish and Star Trek's Klingon, are made for beauty, play or a fictional world. The linguist Arika Okrent's 2009 history of the field closes with a list running to hundreds of projects, most of which attracted few speakers beyond their makers.

A useful contrast is a language nobody designed. When Nicaragua opened a special education center in Managua in 1977, and a vocational school for deaf teenagers in 1980, hundreds of deaf children who had grown up with only home signs were brought together; by 1983 more than 400 were enrolled. They built a shared sign language, and each younger cohort gave it more grammar, such as verb agreement, than the older children had used. Nicaraguan Sign Language emerged rather than being invented, and it shows what children do with language that no planner can.

title: Languages of Pure Reason
description: Seventeenth-century plans to write things instead of words, Wilkins's 1668 Essay, and Leibniz's calculating dream

concepts.title: Writing Things, Not Words
concepts.contentHtml:
In The Advancement of Learning (1605), Francis Bacon reported that China and the kingdoms of the "High Levant," the Far East, wrote in "Characters Real, which express neither letters nor words in gross, but Things or Notions." Peoples who could not understand each other's speech, he noted, could still read each other's writing. The remark helped set off a century of schemes. If Chinese could do it, Europeans reasoned, a scholar might design a script, and even a spoken language, in which every sign named a concept directly and anyone could read it.

Several pressures fed the dream. Latin, the shared language of European learning, was losing ground to vernaculars. Travelers and missionaries were meeting languages by the hundred. The new science wanted names as exact as its measurements, and many blamed the looseness of ordinary words for philosophical quarrels. In a letter to Marin Mersenne of 20 November 1629, René Descartes judged that a truly philosophical language was possible, but only once the true philosophy had been worked out, and he did not expect to see one in use. The London merchant Francis Lodwick published A Common Writing in 1647, and the Scottish teacher George Dalgarno, who worked for a time with John Wilkins in Oxford, produced his Ars Signorum ("Art of Signs") in 1661.

The premise about Chinese was mistaken. Most Chinese characters include a component that signals sound, and they write the words of a particular language rather than pure ideas. But the misunderstanding was productive. It pushed thinkers to ask what a complete, ordered list of all concepts would look like, and that question produced the most ambitious attempt of the century.

concepts.title: Wilkins's Essay of 1668
concepts.contentHtml:
John Wilkins (1614 to 1672) was a founder of the Royal Society and one of its first two secretaries, Oliver Cromwell's brother-in-law, and later Bishop of Chester. In 1662 the Society's council spurred him to write on a universal language. The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed part of the draft, but An Essay towards a Real Character, and a Philosophical Language appeared in 1668, with plant tables by the naturalist John Ray and an alphabetical dictionary compiled by William Lloyd.

Wilkins sorted everything that can be named into 40 genera, each split into differences and then species, and gave every level a sound. Zi is the genus of beasts; Zit the difference "rapacious beasts of the dog kind"; Zitα the species dog. A word was meant to be a definition: knowing how to spell a thing meant knowing its place in the order of nature. He also designed a script of strokes and hooks, the "real character," to write concepts with no spoken form at all.

The flaw is built into the method. Related things get nearly identical names, so a one-letter slip lands on a neighbor. Umberto Eco noticed that Wilkins himself wrote Gαde, barley, where he apparently meant Gαpe, tulip. The tables also froze the science of the 1660s, so any new discovery or regrouping of nature would scramble the vocabulary. The Essay drew interest and later revisers, but it never gained speakers. Its afterlife lay in classification itself: Peter Mark Roget's Thesaurus (1852), which arranges words by concept rather than alphabet, is often described as carrying out a plan of the same kind.

concepts.title: Leibniz's Calculus of Thought, and Borges's Joke
concepts.contentHtml:
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646 to 1716) wanted more than a tidy dictionary. From his De Arte Combinatoria of 1666 onward he sketched a characteristica universalis, a notation for all concepts, paired with a calculus ratiocinator, rules for computing with them. In drafts from about 1679 he gave each simple concept a number, so that a compound concept is the product of its parts: if "animal" is 2 and "rational" is 3, "man" is 6, and whether one concept contains another becomes a question of divisibility. In the 1680s he wrote that with such a language, two philosophers in a dispute could take up their pens and say to each other, Calculemus, "let us calculate."

He never finished it, and in a letter of 1714 he admitted how hard it would be to form. The hope of mechanical reasoning outlived the plan. Gottlob Frege's Begriffsschrift ("concept script," 1879), a founding text of modern logic, is read by some scholars as consciously inspired by it.

One verdict on the whole tradition came from fiction. In "The Analytical Language of John Wilkins," first printed in the Buenos Aires newspaper La Nación on 8 February 1942, Jorge Luis Borges admired Wilkins's ingenuity and then set beside it a Chinese encyclopedia, the Celestial Emporium of Benevolent Knowledge, that divides animals into those belonging to the emperor, embalmed ones, those drawn with a very fine camel-hair brush, and those that from a long way off look like flies. The encyclopedia is Borges's own invention, but his point stands: every classification of the universe is arbitrary and conjectural.

title: Music, Volapük and the First Craze
description: A language you can play on a bugle, a priest's world language, and the quarrel over who owned it

concepts.title: Solresol: A Language You Can Sing
concepts.contentHtml:
François Sudre (1787 to 1862), a violinist trained at the Paris Conservatoire, began in 1817 with a practical question: could the sounds of an instrument carry messages over long distances? From musical signals he worked up a full language built from just seven syllables, the notes of the scale: do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si. Because each syllable can also be a note, a numeral from 1 to 7, a color of the rainbow or a simple written mark, Solresol can be spoken, sung, played, painted, written as numbers or signed with the hands.

Words are short strings of notes. Do means "no," si "yes," re "and." Seven notes allow 49 two-note combinations, 343 of three notes and 2,401 of four, with four-note words grouped into themes by their first note. The best-known trick is reversal: misol means "good" and solmi "bad"; fala is "good" or "tasty" and lafa "bad." Domisol is God, and its reverse, solmido, the Devil. Not every pair works that way: dorefare (neck) and refaredo (wardrobe) are not opposites.

Sudre won real attention. A commission of the Institut de France that included the physicist François Arago praised the system after he submitted it in 1828, the war ministry tested his bugle signals on the Champ-de-Mars, and the jury of the 1855 Universal Exposition voted him 10,000 francs. Admirers reportedly included Victor Hugo, Alphonse de Lamartine and Alexander von Humboldt. His grammar and dictionary, Langue musicale universelle, appeared in 1866, four years after his death, and Boleslas Gajewski's Grammaire du Solresol of 1902 became its standard grammar. It gathered praise, but hardly any speakers.

concepts.title: Volapük: A Priest's World Language
concepts.contentHtml:
Johann Martin Schleyer (1831 to 1912) was the Catholic priest of Litzelstetten, near Konstanz in southern Germany, when, as he told it, a sleepless night in 1879 convinced him that God was calling him to create an international language. He published a sketch that May in Sionsharfe, a Catholic poetry magazine he edited, and a full book in 1880. He called it Volapük, from vol "world" and pük "speech," both bent out of the English words "world" and "speak."

That bending was typical. Schleyer took most roots from English, with some from German, French, Italian, Spanish and Russian, but cut them down toward one syllable and often altered them beyond recognition. The original language had no r, and it used the umlauted vowels ä, ö and ü. Its grammar was elaborate: nouns took four cases, adjectives ended in -ik and adverbs in -o, and by one count a single verb could take 1,584 forms.

For about a decade it spread fast. Congresses met at Friedrichshafen in 1884 and Munich in 1887, both conducted in German; at the third, in Paris in 1889, about 200 delegates did their business entirely in Volapük. By then there were, by one tally, 283 clubs, 25 periodicals and 316 textbooks in 25 languages. Supporters claimed nearly a million learners, a figure no one could check and probably generous. Schleyer's motto, Menade bal, püki bal, means "one humanity, one language."

concepts.title: The Schism
concepts.contentHtml:
Success raised a question Schleyer did not think was open: who owned Volapük? The Munich congress of 1887 set up an International Academy of Volapük to guard and improve the language, and its director became Auguste Kerckhoffs (1835 to 1903), a Dutch-born linguist living in France who lectured for Volapük in France, Spain and Scandinavia. Kerckhoffs is better remembered as a cryptographer. His 1883 essay La Cryptographie militaire set out the principle, still taught, that a cipher should stay secure even if the enemy learns everything about it except the key.

Kerckhoffs and others in the Academy wanted reforms; Schleyer insisted on his rights as the language's author, including a veto over changes. When new statutes passed at the 1889 congress took that veto away and the Academy blocked his own proposals, Schleyer dismissed it, and in 1890 he appointed a rival academy of 49 loyal members, which soon faded. The movement fell into disarray, and many Volapükists drifted to a newer rival from Warsaw, Esperanto, which was simpler and which its author had placed in the public domain.

The original Academy kept reforming until its work became a different language. Under Waldemar Rosenberger, director from 1892, it produced Idiom Neutral, set out in a dictionary and grammar of 1902 and 1903, and in 1908 it switched again, to Giuseppe Peano's Latino sine flexione. In 1931 the Dutch Volapükist Arie de Jong published a simplified revision that restored r, so that "rain" became rein instead of lömib. Around 2000 an estimated 20 people could speak Volapük. Its most lasting trace may be an insult: in Danish, volapyk means gibberish.

title: Esperanto: The Hope That Lasted
description: Zamenhof's 1887 booklet, a grammar built from regular endings, and a community that outlived two dictatorships

concepts.title: Doktoro Esperanto
concepts.contentHtml:
Ludwik Lejzer Zamenhof was born on 15 December 1859 in Białystok, then in the Russian Empire. In a letter of about 1895 he recalled a town divided among Russians, Poles, Germans and Jews, each group speaking its own language and hostile to the others. He grew up speaking Yiddish and Russian, used Polish daily and learned German from his father, and he came to believe that a neutral second language, belonging to no nation, could ease such hatreds. By 1878, he later wrote, the language had seemed ready, yet he spent six more years perfecting and testing it while he studied medicine.

On 26 July 1887 the Warsaw publisher Chaim Kelter issued a small book in Russian titled International Language, financed with help from the family of Klara Silbernik, whom Zamenhof married that year. Esperantists call it the Unua Libro, the "First Book." It set out 16 grammar rules and 917 roots, and it was signed with a pseudonym, Doktoro Esperanto, "Doctor One-Who-Hopes," which became the language's name. Polish, French and German editions followed before the year was out.

Two choices set it apart from Volapük. Zamenhof gave up all rights, putting the language in the public domain, and he froze a core. In 1905 the first World Esperanto Congress, at Boulogne-sur-Mer in France, drew 688 people of 20 nationalities and declared the Fundamento de Esperanto binding: speakers could add words but not rewrite the base. A committee organized by Louis Couturat in 1907 backed a reformed offshoot, Ido, which drew away some prominent supporters but never displaced the original.

concepts.title: How Esperanto Works
concepts.contentHtml:
Esperanto's grammar is short because its endings carry the load. Every noun ends in -o, every adjective in -a, and adverbs formed from roots in -e: hundo "dog," bona "good," bone "well." The plural adds -j (bonaj hundoj, "good dogs"), and the direct object adds -n, which frees word order: la hundo vidas la katon and la katon vidas la hundo both mean "the dog sees the cat." Adjectives agree with their nouns in number and case. There is one article, la, which never changes, and nouns have no grammatical gender.

Verbs never change for person. The infinitive ends in -i (vidi, "to see"), and five endings do the rest: -as present, -is past, -os future, -us conditional and -u for commands and wishes. So mi vidis is "I saw" and ili vidos "they will see." Stress always falls on the second-to-last syllable, and the 28-letter alphabet is spelled as pronounced, including six letters with marks: ĉ, ĝ, ĥ, ĵ, ŝ and ŭ.

Vocabulary grows from roots by fixed affixes. Mal- makes an opposite: bona good, malbona bad; varma warm, malvarma cold. -in- makes a female form (patro father, patrino mother), -ej- a place (lerni to learn, lernejo school), -et- something smaller and -eg- something bigger. Critics point to the costs: the roots are overwhelmingly European, the accusative trips up many learners, and building female words from male ones writes a bias into the words for people. Supporters answer that it is still far quicker to learn than any national language, a claim that is hard to test rigorously.

concepts.title: Banned, Purged, and Still Spoken
concepts.contentHtml:
Its internationalism made Esperanto suspect to dictators. In Mein Kampf Hitler cast a universal language such as Esperanto as a tool of Jewish world domination. In Nazi Germany planned languages were effectively prohibited in May 1935, and in June 1936 Heinrich Himmler banned the Esperanto associations. Zamenhof, who died in Warsaw in 1917, did not live to see it, but all three of his children were murdered in the Holocaust. His son Adam, an eye doctor like his father, was killed at Palmiry in January 1940, and his daughters Zofia and Lidia, Lidia a noted teacher of Esperanto, were sent to the Treblinka death camp in 1942.

The Soviet Union first tolerated and even encouraged the movement, then turned on it in the Great Purge, when contacts with foreign correspondents made Esperantists easy to accuse of espionage. Ernest Drezen, president of the Soviet Esperantist Union, was arrested on 17 April 1937 and shot on 27 October 1937; he was rehabilitated in 1957. Esperanto was effectively banned in the USSR until 1956.

It survived anyway. UNESCO passed a resolution in its support at Montevideo in 1954, and estimates of speakers today run from tens of thousands to about two million, depending on what counts as speaking. Some families raise children in it: a 2004 estimate counted about 1,000 such families, and the Nobel-winning pharmacologist Daniel Bovet grew up with it. A 2001 study by the linguist Benjamin Bergen found native-speaking children reshaping the language, for instance using the accusative much less when their other language lacked one; Jouko Lindstedt has argued that this reflects transfer from those languages rather than a new native grammar.

title: Logic and the Shape of Thought
description: Languages built to test whether the words we have shape the thoughts we can think

concepts.title: Loglan: A Language to Test Whorf
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1955 James Cooke Brown (1921 to 2000), an American sociologist who also designed the board game Careers, began a language meant as an experiment. The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, named for the linguists Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, holds in its strong form that the language you speak shapes or limits how you think. Brown reasoned that a fair test needed a language unlike any natural one. If people who learned a tongue built on formal logic began to think differently, that would count for the hypothesis; if they did not, against it.

He called it Loglan, from "logical language," and introduced it to a wide audience in a 1960 article in Scientific American. Its grammar follows predicate logic: a word for giving is a predicate with numbered slots for giver, gift and receiver, and words for "and," "or" and "if" behave as logicians define them rather than loosely, as in English. To make roots memorable for as many people as possible, Brown built each one from the words for that idea in eight widely spoken languages: English, Mandarin, Hindi, Russian, Spanish, French, Japanese and German. Robert Heinlein mentioned Loglan in his novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress (1966).

No decisive test came out of it. Its community stayed small and self-selected, and Brown kept tight control. He founded The Loglan Institute and kept claiming legal restrictions on the language and its materials, which frustrated volunteers who wanted to build on it freely. In 1987 a group of them broke away to start again.

concepts.title: Lojban: No Ambiguity Allowed
concepts.contentHtml:
The breakaway Logical Language Group, founded in 1987 in Washington, D.C., with Bob LeChevalier as its president, rebuilt the language under a new name, Lojban, from its own words logji "logic" and bangu "language." The US Patent and Trademark Office eventually upheld that "Loglan" itself could not be trademarked. Lojban's root words, the gismu, number about 1,350, all five letters long in the shape CVCCV or CCVCV. A computer generated each one by blending the words for the concept in Mandarin, English, Hindi, Spanish, Russian and Arabic, weighted by numbers of speakers.

Each root is a predicate with fixed slots. Klama means "x1 goes to x2 from x3 by route x4 using vehicle x5," and a sentence fills as many slots as it needs. Mi prami do is "I love you." Feelings get their own small words, called attitudinals: .oi signals pain or complaint, .u'u regret. Spelling and sound match one to one, so any spoken sentence can be written down exactly.

The central claim is that Lojban's grammar is syntactically unambiguous: its rules have been tested by computer so that a grammatical sentence parses in only one way. That does not make meaning precise, since a word can still be vague, but a sentence like "I saw the man with the telescope," which has two readings in English, must be built one way or the other. The design was frozen in 1997 with The Complete Lojban Language by John Woldemar Cowan, a reference grammar of more than 600 pages. Fluent speakers remain few, so Lojban has not delivered a Whorf test either.

concepts.title: Láadan: A Language for Women
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1982 the linguist and science-fiction writer Suzette Haden Elgin (1936 to 2015), who earned her PhD at the University of California, San Diego, and later taught at San Diego State University, began a different Whorf test. She asked whether a language designed around women's perceptions would change the culture that used it, with a subsidiary idea that Western natural languages may suit men's perceptions better than women's. She called it Láadan and gave it to the women linguists of her novel Native Tongue (1984), followed by The Judas Rose (1987) and Earthsong (1993).

Láadan puts the speaker's stance on the surface. A sentence can open with a particle that says what kind of speech act it is: bíi for a statement, báa for a question, bóo for a request. Another particle marks the evidence behind a claim: wa means the speaker perceived it herself, wáa that she assumes it is true because she trusts the source. Affixes mark feelings, such as -lh- for dislike. Active sentences run verb, subject, object, and the language has two tones and five vowels.

Elgin reported in 1987 that men mostly found it impractical, while women were more positive; Anthony Burgess called it "ingenious" in a 1985 review but predicted "it's not going to work." No speech community formed that was large enough to test her question. That fits where research on the Sapir-Whorf idea has ended up: few linguists now accept that language fixes what we can think, while experiments do find smaller effects, such as faster discrimination between colors that one's language names separately.

title: Languages for Worlds, and the Smallest Language
description: Tolkien's Elvish, Klingon from Star Trek, and Toki Pona's roughly 120 words

concepts.title: Tolkien: The Languages Came First
concepts.contentHtml:
J. R. R. Tolkien began inventing an Elvish language as a schoolboy at King Edward's School in Birmingham, around 1910 to 1911, and kept revising his languages for the rest of his life. He was a professional philologist, and when he began building his mythology, Finnish, which he said had "quite intoxicated" him, was the dominant influence on his first Elvish tongue, called Qenya by about 1915 and later spelled Quenya, his "Elven-latin." A second, Sindarin, he gave a Welsh-like sound, with sound changes deliberately resembling those that produced medieval and modern Welsh from ancient Celtic.

In a 1955 letter to his American publisher, Houghton Mifflin, he put the order of things bluntly: the "stories" were made "rather to provide a world for the languages than the reverse." Middle-earth's histories exist partly so that his languages would have peoples, migrations and sound changes to explain them. Frodo's greeting to the Elves in The Lord of the Rings, Elen síla lúmenn' omentielvo, "a star shines on the hour of our meeting," is Quenya.

He described the hobby in a talk, "A Secret Vice," given on 29 November 1931 to a literary society at Pembroke College, Oxford, and first printed in 1983. He separated such private art languages from auxiliary ones like Esperanto, which he praised, and argued that "your language construction will breed a mythology." Because he revised endlessly, there is no single finished Elvish grammar. Scholars are still publishing his linguistic papers in journals such as Vinyar Tengwar and Parma Eldalamberon, and fans who write Elvish today are partly reconstructing it.

concepts.title: Klingon: Built to Sound Alien
concepts.contentHtml:
Klingon began as a few harsh-sounding words devised by the actor James Doohan, Scotty in Star Trek, and Jon Povill for Star Trek: The Motion Picture (1979). For Star Trek III: The Search for Spock (1984) the producers commissioned Marc Okrand, a linguist whose 1977 Berkeley dissertation described Mutsun, an extinct Ohlone language of California, and who had already dubbed Vulcan lines for Star Trek II. He built a full language and published The Klingon Dictionary in 1985.

Okrand made it sound alien by breaking the habits of natural languages. Its consonants form a lopsided set that includes tlh and a deep-throated Q, and its basic word order is object, verb, subject, an order very rare among human languages, though attested in a few, such as Hixkaryana in the Amazon. Greetings are blunt: the nearest thing to hello, nuqneH, means "what do you want?" and Qapla', "success," serves as goodbye.

Fans made it real. The Klingon Language Institute, founded by Lawrence M. Schoen in Pennsylvania in 1992, has published Klingon versions of Hamlet, Much Ado About Nothing, the Tao Te Ching and Gilgamesh, and Duolingo opened a course in 2018. Fluency is rare: Arika Okrent estimated in 2009 that 20 to 30 people spoke it well. The linguist d'Armond Speers tried raising his son with Klingon; the boy stopped answering in it, and Speers switched to English. Screen languages became paid work: in 2009 HBO found David J. Peterson through a Language Creation Society contest to build Dothraki for Game of Thrones.

concepts.title: Toki Pona: How Little Can a Language Hold
concepts.contentHtml:
Toki Pona went the opposite way from Lojban's 1,350 roots. The Canadian translator Sonja Lang began it in 2001, during a period of depression, as a way to simplify her thoughts, and posted an early version online that year. It draws partly on Taoist philosophy and was designed with the Sapir-Whorf idea in mind. Her book Toki Pona: The Language of Good (2014) has about 120 core words, and her Toki Pona Dictionary (2021) lists 137 "essential" ones. The sound system has just 14 phonemes: nine consonants and five vowels.

The name shows the method: toki "language, talk" plus pona "good, simple." With so few roots, speakers build meaning by combining. A friend is jan pona, "good person." Alcohol is telo nasa, "strange liquid." Green is laso kasi, roughly "plant blue." Counting is deliberately crude: wan one, tu two, tu wan three, tu tu four, and in Lang's book luka ("hand") five and mute ("many") twenty. Large numbers are possible but tiresome, by design.

The price is vagueness: telo nasa could be any odd liquid, and the listener must lean on context. Yet Toki Pona has done what most conlangs never do and built a lasting community. Lang said in 2007 that at least 100 people spoke it fluently; a 2021 estimate put users between 500 and 5,000. In January 2022 the ISO 639-3 standard gave it its own code, tok, joining Esperanto, Klingon and Lojban among the invented languages with one.
